From 1 August 2019, the academic integrity policy provides a framework for the 
management of academic misconduct. The purpose of the policy and associated 
procedures is to ensure that Cardiff University can discharge effectively its 
responsibilities to all students and address any concerns raised, fairly and 
effectively.

Introduction

1.1 The University has fundamental core values that we expect students to 
abide by in their academic work. These include integrity, honesty, openness, 
rigour, accountability, care, and respect. It is essential to the functioning of 
our academic community that students behave in a way that is consistent 
with these core values in all aspects of study and research. A student is 
expected to maintain high standards of academic practice and not engage in 
academic misconduct.

Academic Integrity Policy
Section 2 Definition of Academic Misconduct 


2.1 When your action(s) or inaction(s) raises a concern that you might be 
engaging in academic misconduct, this will be investigated as a breach of 
academic integrity. Academic misconduct can take place irrespective of 
whether your actions or inactions were intended to gain an unfair advantage 
or not. Academic misconduct includes, but is not limited to the following:

Academic Integrity Policy
Section 2.1 Plagiarism: the use of someone else's words, ideas, intellectual 
property, or work, without proper acknowledgment by use of correct 
referencing conventions, or necessary permissions. Words or ideas 
may include: text (including paraphrasing), diagrams, formulae, 
software.

.2 Self-plagiarism: when work is reproduced or re-presented for 
assessment when it has already been part of another assessment. 
This includes work on your current programme of study or a previous 
programme of study at the University or at another educational 
institution.

.4 Collusion: presenting work as your own when it has been produced 
by, or with, someone else, or allowing work to be submitted in 
someone else's name.

3 Definition of Academic Misconduct in Research 


3.1 All students taking part in research are expected to observe the highest 
standards of professional behaviour, rigour and integrity in conducting and 
presenting their research. It is the responsibility of students undertaking 
research to be aware of their commitments and the expectations of the 
University in this regard, as outlined in the Research Integrity and 
Governance Code of Practice. Contraventions of the Research Integrity and 
Governance Code of Practice may amount to academic misconduct. 
Students should also comply with the expectations and requirements of 
funding and regulatory bodies, sponsors and relevant legislation, including 
research ethics requirements.

Academic Integrity Policy
Section 3.2 In addition to relevant examples of academic misconduct listed above 
(plagiarism, collusion), research misconduct encompasses, but is not limited 
to, the following: 
- Fabrication - includes the creation of false data or other aspects of 
research, including documentation and participant consent. 
- Falsification - includes the inappropriate manipulation and/or selection 
of data, imagery, research processes, materials and/or consents. This 
includes changing or omitting data or results so that the research is not 
accurately represented in the research record. 
- Misrepresentation of: 
− 
Data - including suppression of relevant results/data or knowingly, 
recklessly or negligently presenting a flawed interpretation of data 
− 
Involvement - including inappropriate claims to authorship or 
attribution of work and denial of authorship/attribution to persons 
who have made an appropriate contribution 
− 
Interests - including failure to declare a conflict of interest/a 
competing interest, qualifications, experience and/or credentials of 
publication history, including undisclosed duplication of publication
section_heading: In addition to relevant examples of academic misconduct listed above

text:
- Mismanagement or inadequate preservation of data and/or primary 
materials - non-compliance with University and/or funders' 
requirements for the management or preservation of data and/or 
primary material. 
- Failure to meet legal, ethical, or professional requirements, including: 
− 
not observing legal, ethical and other requirements for human 
research participants, animal subjects, or human organs or tissue 
used in research, or for the protection of the environment 
(including a failure to obtain appropriate ethical 
review/commencing human research without having first obtained 
a favourable ethical opinion (where such an opinion was 
required)) 
− 
breach of duty of care for humans involved in research whether 
deliberately, recklessly or negligently, including failure to obtain 
appropriate informed consent (where required) 
− 
misuse of personal data, failure to ensure the proper handling of 
privileged or private information on individuals collected during the 
research.

Academic Integrity Policy
Section 3.3 Any misconduct during research activity that is not dealt with by the relevant 
Academic Misconduct Procedure will be dealt with under the Student 
Conduct Procedure or, where the individual concerned is a staff candidate, 
the Procedures for Dealing with Allegations of Misconduct in Academic 
Research.

3.4 Honest errors and differences in, for example, interpretations do not 
constitute research misconduct. Similarly, it does not include what is no 
more than academically poor research.

Introduction 
 
 
These Academic Regulations and associated policies and procedures provide a 
framework for the development, management and delivery of programmes and study 
at Cardiff University. The purpose of the regulations and associated policies is to 
ensure that Cardiff University can discharge effectively its responsibilities to all 
students fairly and effectively and to ensure that the standards of awards are 
consistent with the relevant national qualification frameworks. 
The 2025/26 Academic Regulations apply to students who have enrolled, or reenrolled since 1 August 2026. For students who have not yet enrolled this academic 
year, the 2024/25 Academic Regulations will apply. 
The regulations have been presented using the following structure: 
- 
Academic Governance 
- 
Admissions 
- 
Awards and Programmes 
- 
Assessment 
- 
Student Study and Engagement 
- 
Student Conduct 
- 
Student Complaints and Appeals 
 
Associated policies and procedures have been aligned with this structure. There are 
links to the appropriate policies and procedures and these can be found in the 
Sources of Further Information section. 
If you are a disabled student and require adjustments to these regulations or 
procedures to be able to fully engage with the process, please contact the Academic 
Registrar to identify any reasonable adjustments which can be made to support your 
engagement. 
University officers may nominate alternates to act on their behalf.

Institutional Oversight 
 
The Academic Regulations are approved by Senate on the recommendation of the 
Academic Standards and Quality Committee (ASQC). The regulations will be kept 
under regular review to ensure they continue both to support internal processes to 
function efficiently and effectively, and to fully meet the principles of the UK Quality 
Code for Higher Education. Sector-Agreed Principles 
Principle 1: Taking a strategic approach to managing quality and standards 
Providers demonstrate they have a strategic approach to securing academic 
standards and assuring and enhancing quality that is embedded across the 
organisation. Principle 2: Engaging students as partners 
Providers take deliberate steps to engage students as active partners in assuring 
and enhancing the quality of the student learning experience. Engagement happens 
individually and collectively to influence all levels of study and decision making. Enhancements identified through student engagement activities are implemented, 
where appropriate, and communicated to staff and students. Principle 3: Resourcing delivery of a high-quality learning experience 
Providers plan, secure and maintain resources relating to learning, technology, 
facilities and staffing to enable the delivery and enhancement of an accessible, 
innovative and high-quality learning experience for students that aligns with the 
provider's strategy and the composition of the student body. Principle 4: Using data to inform and evaluate quality 
Providers collect, analyse and utilise qualitative and quantitative data at provider, 
departmental, programme and module levels. These analyses inform decisionmaking with the aim of enhancing practices and processes relating to teaching, 
learning and the wider student experience. Principle 5: Monitoring, evaluating and enhancing provision 
Providers regularly monitor and review their provision to secure academic standards 
and enhance quality. Deliberate steps are taken to engage and involve students, 
staff and external expertise in monitoring and evaluation activity. The outcomes and 
impact of these activities are considered at provider level to drive reflection and 
enhancement across the provider.

transparent, fair and inclusive. Providers maintain and publish accurate, relevant and 
accessible information about their provision, enabling students to make informed 
choices about their studies and future aspirations. Principle 10: Supporting students to achieve their potential 
Providers facilitate a framework of support for students that enables them to have a 
high-quality learning experience and achieve their potential as they progress in their 
studies. The support structure scaffolds the academic, personal and professional 
learning journey, enabling students to recognise and articulate their progress and 
achievements. Principle 11: Teaching, learning and assessment 
Providers facilitate a collaborative and inclusive approach that enables students to 
have a high-quality learning experience and to progress through their studies.

Section 1 Governance 
Academic Governance 
Academic Management Regulations

1 Governance 


1.1 The constitutional framework within which the University operates is based 
upon its Royal Charter and the supporting Statutes and Ordinances. These 
Academic Regulations, relating to academic management, supplement the 
content of the Charter, Statues and Ordinances. 
Council is the governing body and, as such, the supreme authority of the 
University. It has the ultimate power of decision in all matters affecting the 
University (Ordinance 4). 
The Senate is our chief academic authority and is responsible, on behalf of 
the Council, for determining educational policy (Ordinance 5). 
The Education and Student Experience Committee is responsible for 
advising the University on all matters relating to education and the student 
experience across the full range of its provision for students (Ordinance 
10). 
The Academic Standards and Quality Committee is responsible for advising 
the University on all matters relating to the promotion of academic quality 
and standards (Ordinance 10). 
The University Awards and Progress Committee, under authority delegated 
to it by Senate and Council, receives recommendations from Examining 
Boards and admits those qualified to degrees, certificates, diplomas or 
other academic award of the University (Ordinance 10).

1.1 The University reserves the right to add to, delete or make reasonable 
changes to the Regulations where in the opinion of the University this will 
assist in the proper delivery of education. Changes are usually made for one 
or more of the following reasons: 
 
a) 
To review and update the Regulations to ensure they are fit for 
purpose; 
b) 
To reflect changes in the external environment, including legal or 
regulatory changes, changes to funding or financial arrangements or 
changes to government policy, requirements or guidance; 
c) 
To incorporate sector guidance or best practice; 
d) 
To incorporate feedback from students; and/or 
e) 
To aid clarity or consistency of approach.

Section 1.2 The University will consult the Students' Union Elected Officers before 
making any substantive changes to the Regulations.

year, although a change may be introduced during the academic year where 
the University reasonably considers this to be in the interests of students or 
where this is required by law or other exceptional circumstances. The 
University will take all reasonable steps to minimise disruption to students 
wherever reasonably possible, for example, by giving reasonable notice of 
changes to Regulations before they take effect, or by phasing in the 
changes, if appropriate.

Admissions Regulations 
 
 
Institutional Oversight 
The Admissions Regulations and associated policies and procedures have been 
approved by Senate. The regulations and policies will be kept under regular review 
to ensure they continue both to support internal processes to function efficiently and 
effectively, and to fully meet the principles of the UK Quality Code for Higher 
Education, with particular reference to the key practices set out in principle 9. 
Principle 9 - Recruiting, selecting and admitting students 
Providers operate recruitment, selection and admissions processes that are 
transparent, fair and inclusive. Providers maintain and publish accurate, relevant 
and accessible information about their provision, enabling students to make 
informed choices about their studies and future aspirations. 
Key practices 
a. Policies and procedures for application, recruitment, selection and admission 
to programmes are reliable, fair, transparent and accessible, including 
processes for the recognition of prior learning. Similar and proportionate 
arrangements are in place for modules and other units of study. 
b. Providers offer information that supports prospective students, and their 
advisors for recruitment and widening access purposes, in making informed 
decisions. Providers meet their legal and regulatory obligations in relation to 
the information presented about themselves and their provision or any 
changes they make to programmes and modules. 
c. Staff, student representatives and external partners engaged in the delivery of 
recruitment, selection, admissions and widening access processes are 
appropriately trained and resourced. 
d. All teams involved in the application, selection and admissions processes 
ensure information about the applicant journey is consistent and clear. Specific 
elements of the selection process are clearly defined and any programme or 
module changes that can impact decision making are communicated swiftly 
and consistently to enable all parties to exercise informed choice.

2.1 The University has general entrance requirements in place to ensure that 
applicants have the necessary prerequisites to succeed on a programme at 
the University. The entry requirements set must satisfy the University that 
applicants will be of appropriate academic standard to complete the 
programme.

that will enable them to benefit fully from their programme; the level required 
will vary by programme. The level will be specified with reference to a GCSE

degree programme taught through the medium of English, or an IELTS test. 
A full list of acceptable equivalent tests and qualifications, along with the 
scores applicants need to achieve, is published alongside Admissions 
policies on the University website.

Undergraduate degree programmes 
Candidates for undergraduate degree programmes are required either to 
hold qualifications at Credit and Qualifications Framework (CQFW) level 3 
(or above) or equivalent as determined by Cardiff University in its 
qualification equivalency guides, or to have been assessed by the Academic 
School as having equivalent professional experience/learning. 
Postgraduate taught degree programmes 
Candidates for postgraduate taught degree programmes are required either 
to hold qualifications at Credit and Qualifications Framework (CQFW) level 6 
(or above) or equivalent as determined by Cardiff University in its 
qualification equivalency guides, or to have been assessed by the Academic 
School as having equivalent professional experience/learning. 
Research degree programmes 
Candidates for postgraduate research degrees are required to hold 
qualifications at Credit and Qualifications Framework (CQFW) level 6 (or 
above) or equivalent as determined by Cardiff University in its qualification 
equivalency guides. Irrespective of a candidate's qualifications, the School 
concerned must satisfy itself that a candidate is of the required academic 
standard to complete the programme of research proposed 
Candidates for the degree of MD must have qualified for the degrees of 
Bachelor of Medicine and Bachelor of Surgery at least 3 years prior to 
admission. 
For funded research places, entry requirements may be set in line with the 
funding requirements.

Section 1.3 The Credit and Qualifications Framework for Wales (CQFW) provides the 
common framework that operates across Wales through which the level and 
volume of credit-based learning is defined.

1.4 Credit is an award made to a student in recognition of the achievement of 
designated learning outcomes at a specified credit level. The amount of 
credit attributed to a module is based upon an estimation of the learning time 
taken by the average student to achieve the learning outcomes specified. 
Twenty credits comprises a minimum of two hundred study hours including 
associated contact hours, independent study and assessment.

Section 1.5 The credit level is an indicator of the relative demand, complexity, and depth 
of learning, and of learner autonomy. It is defined as follows: 
CQFW Level 3: Credit normally acquired on foundation programmes, the 
standard of which is equivalent to GCE A Level, and which would prepare 
students for entry to undergraduate degree study; 
CQFW Level 4: Credit normally acquired in the first year of undergraduate 
programmes, which is appropriate to the award of a University Certificate of 
Higher Education; 
CQFW Level 5: Credit normally acquired in the second year of 
undergraduate programmes, which is appropriate to the award of a 
University Diploma of Higher Education; 
CQFW Level 6: Credit normally acquired in the final year of undergraduate 
programmes, which is appropriate to the award of an honours degree; 
CQFW Level 7: Credit normally acquired in taught postgraduate 
programmes, which is appropriate to the award of an Integrated Master's 
degree or of a Master's degree; 
CQFW Level 8: Credit normally acquired in postgraduate research 
programmes and appropriate to the award of a doctorate.

1.6 A Graduate Diploma will be the appropriate award to a student admitted with 
recognition of prior learning (credit transfer) to a Cardiff University

Taught Programme Regulations 
 
 
The Regulations for Taught Programmes have been approved by Senate. The 
regulations will be kept under regular review to ensure they continue both to support 
internal processes to function efficiently and effectively, and to fully meet the 
principles of the UK Quality Code for Higher Education, with particular reference to 
the key practices set out in Principle 11. Principle 11 - Teaching, learning and assessment 
Providers facilitate a collaborative and inclusive approach that enables students to 
have a high-quality learning experience and to progress through their studies. All 
students are supported to develop and demonstrate academic and professional 
skills and competencies. Assessment employs a variety of methods, embodying the 
values of academic integrity, producing outcomes that are comparable across the 
UK and recognised globally. Key Practices 
a. Learning and assessment at all levels is informed by research and/or scholarship. Teaching, learning and assessment align to ensure students can demonstrate 
their achievements, reflect on and reinforce their prior learning, skills and 
knowledge, and fulfil their potential. b. Students are given clear information about the intended modular and/or 
programme learning outcomes and the purpose of assessment and are enabled 
to use feedback/ feedforward to support further learning. c. Staff involved in facilitating learning and supervising research are appropriately 
qualified and supported to enhance their teaching and supervisory practice. Research degrees are delivered in supportive environments that are conducive to 
learning and research. d. Students are enabled and encouraged to take responsibility for their own learning 
and to take an active role in shaping and enhancing the learning process. Providers offer ongoing advice and guidance about academic integrity to ensure 
that students and staff understand what is expected of them. e. As students move through their learning journey, they are given the opportunity 
and support to transition effectively between academic levels, further study and 
employment.

Section 2.4 Within each stage of a programme, a diet of approved modules must be 
specified. The designation of modules will fall into the following types: 
 
Required Module: A module that all students registered on a particular 
programme must take and must pass by achieving the minimum pass mark. 
If students do not pass a required module, they will not be able to progress 
to the next stage of the programme, nor graduate from the programme with 
the intended award. 
 
Core Module: A module that all students registered on a particular 
programme must take. 
 
Optional Module: A module which is optional for students registered on a 
programme. 
 
Co-requisite module: A module that must be studied concurrently by 
students registered on a particular programme. 
 
Precursor module: A module a student must have completed in order to 
proceed to a subsequent specified module, but for which credit may not yet 
have been awarded prior to the commencement of the subsequent module. 
 
Prerequisite module: A module in which a student must be required to 
have received credit in order to proceed to a subsequent specified module. 
 
No module which is timetabled for the Autumn Semester can be a 
prerequisite for entry into a module which is scheduled for the Spring 
Semester immediately following.

Research Programmes 
Research Degree Regulations 
 
 
 
Institutional Oversight 
The Research Degree Regulations have been approved by Senate. The regulations will be 
kept under regular review to ensure they continue both to support internal processes to 
function efficiently and effectively, and to fully meet the principles of the UK Quality Code for 
Higher Education, with particular reference to the key practices set out in Principle 11. Principle 11 - Teaching, learning and assessment 
Providers facilitate a collaborative and inclusive approach that enables students to 
have a high-quality learning experience and to progress through their studies. All 
students are supported to develop and demonstrate academic and professional 
skills and competencies. Assessment employs a variety of methods, embodying the 
values of academic integrity, producing outcomes that are comparable across the 
UK and recognised globally. Key Practices 
a. Learning and assessment at all levels is informed by research and/or scholarship. Teaching, learning and assessment align to ensure students can demonstrate 
their achievements, reflect on and reinforce their prior learning, skills and 
knowledge, and fulfil their potential. b. Students are given clear information about the intended modular and/or 
programme learning outcomes and the purpose of assessment and are enabled 
to use feedback/ feedforward to support further learning. c. Staff involved in facilitating learning and supervising research are appropriately 
qualified and supported to enhance their teaching and supervisory practice. Research degrees are delivered in supportive environments that are conducive to 
learning and research. d. Students are enabled and encouraged to take responsibility for their own learning 
and to take an active role in shaping and enhancing the learning process. Providers offer ongoing advice and guidance about academic integrity to ensure 
that students and staff understand what is expected of them. e. As students move through their learning journey, they are given the opportunity 
and support to transition effectively between academic levels, further study and 
employment.

Regulations for PhD by Published Works 
 
 
Institutional Oversight 
The Regulations for PhD by Published Works have been approved by Senate. The 
regulations will be kept under regular review to ensure they continue both to support internal 
processes to function efficiently and effectively, and to fully meet the principles of the UK 
Quality Code for Higher Education, with particular reference to the key practices set out in 
Principle 11. Principle 11 - Teaching, learning and assessment 
Providers facilitate a collaborative and inclusive approach that enables students to 
have a high-quality learning experience and to progress through their studies. All 
students are supported to develop and demonstrate academic and professional 
skills and competencies. Assessment employs a variety of methods, embodying the 
values of academic integrity, producing outcomes that are comparable across the 
UK and recognised globally. Key Practices 
a. Learning and assessment at all levels is informed by research and/or scholarship. Teaching, learning and assessment align to ensure students can demonstrate 
their achievements, reflect on and reinforce their prior learning, skills and 
knowledge, and fulfil their potential. b. Students are given clear information about the intended modular and/or 
programme learning outcomes and the purpose of assessment and are enabled 
to use feedback/ feedforward to support further learning. c. Staff involved in facilitating learning and supervising research are appropriately 
qualified and supported to enhance their teaching and supervisory practice. Research degrees are delivered in supportive environments that are conducive to 
learning and research. d. Students are enabled and encouraged to take responsibility for their own learning 
and to take an active role in shaping and enhancing the learning process. Providers offer ongoing advice and guidance about academic integrity to ensure 
that students and staff understand what is expected of them. e. As students move through their learning journey, they are given the opportunity 
and support to transition effectively between academic levels, further study and 
employment.

Section 6 Extenuating Circumstances 


6.1 The University recognises that students will on occasion have personal 
circumstances which may impact on their studies. Extenuating 
Circumstances are defined as those that are: 
- severe and exceptional; and 
- unforeseen or unavoidable; and 
- close in time to the assessment, or where the student can 
demonstrate that the circumstances continued to have an impact on 
academic performance in the assessment.

6.2 Extenuating circumstances will be considered to have had an adverse 
impact on the student's academic performance in assessment and/or have 
prevented a student from submitting a coursework assessment and/or 
attending a scheduled assessment.

Research Degree Assessment Regulations 
 
 
Institutional Oversight 
The Research Degree Assessment Regulations have been approved by Senate. The regulations will be kept under regular review to ensure they continue both to 
support internal processes to function efficiently and effectively, and to fully meet the 
principles of the UK Quality Code for Higher Education, with particular reference to 
the key practices set out in Principle 11. Principle 11 - Teaching, learning and assessment 
Providers facilitate a collaborative and inclusive approach that enables students to 
have a high-quality learning experience and to progress through their studies. All 
students are supported to develop and demonstrate academic and professional 
skills and competencies. Assessment employs a variety of methods, embodying the 
values of academic integrity, producing outcomes that are comparable across the 
UK and recognised globally. Key Practices 
a. Learning and assessment at all levels is informed by research and/or scholarship. Teaching, learning and assessment align to ensure students can demonstrate 
their achievements, reflect on and reinforce their prior learning, skills and 
knowledge, and fulfil their potential. b. Students are given clear information about the intended modular and/or 
programme learning outcomes and the purpose of assessment and are enabled 
to use feedback/ feedforward to support further learning. c. Staff involved in facilitating learning and supervising research are appropriately 
qualified and supported to enhance their teaching and supervisory practice. Research degrees are delivered in supportive environments that are conducive to 
learning and research. d. Students are enabled and encouraged to take responsibility for their own learning 
and to take an active role in shaping and enhancing the learning process. Providers offer ongoing advice and guidance about academic integrity to ensure 
that students and staff understand what is expected of them. e. As students move through their learning journey, they are given the opportunity 
and support to transition effectively between academic levels, further study and 
employment.

Student Study and Engagement Regulations 
 
 
Institutional Oversight 
The Student Study and Engagement Regulations have been approved by Senate. 
The regulations will be kept under regular review to ensure they continue both to 
support internal processes to function efficiently and effectively, and to fully meet the 
principles of the UK Quality Code for Higher Education, with particular reference to 
the key practices set out in Principle 10. 
Principle 10 - Supporting students to achieve their potential 
Providers facilitate a framework of support for students that enables them to have a 
high-quality learning experience and achieve their potential as they progress in their 
studies. The support structure scaffolds the academic, personal and professional 
learning journey, enabling students to recognise and articulate their progress and 
achievements. 
Key Practices 
a. Accessible, relevant, accurate and timely information is offered to students and 
the staff supporting them throughout the learning journey about the provider, 
programme of study, wider opportunities for development and availability of 
support services. 
b. All students are supported at key transition points throughout their journey, with 
their specific needs and requirements met and their pathways into learning 
recognised. 
c. Students and staff are aware of the ongoing academic, professional and pastoral 
services and activities available, and students are encouraged to access these 
opportunities and support throughout their learning journey. 
d. Staff are appropriately qualified, trained and supported to deliver high-quality 
learning and support for all students, particularly those with specific needs and 
requirements. 
e. Students and staff recognise that activities offered outside the formal curriculum 
are beneficial for promoting students' sense of belonging, as well as providing 
opportunities to broaden their skills and achievements, complementing their 
formal studies.

Student Conduct Regulations 
 
Institutional Oversight 
The Student Conduct Regulations have been approved by Senate. The regulations 
will be kept under regular review to ensure they continue both to support internal 
processes to function efficiently and effectively, and to fully meet the requirements of 
the OIA Good Practice Framework for handling complaints and academic appeals, 
and the UK Quality Code for Higher Education, with particular reference to the key 
practices set out in Principle 12. 
Principle 12 - Operating concerns, complaints and appeals processes 
Providers operate processes for complaints and appeals that are robust, fair, 
transparent and accessible, and clearly articulated to staff and students. Policies and 
processes for concerns, complaints and appeals are regularly reviewed and the 
outcomes are used to support the enhancement of provision and the student 
experience. 
Key Practices 
a. Policies and processes for concerns, complaints and appeals are accessible, 
robust and inclusive, and enable early resolution wherever possible and include 
information relating to recruitment, selection and admission. 
b. Concerns, complaints and appeals policies and procedures, including information 
about them, are clear and transparent to students, those advising them and those 
implementing the processes. Formal and informal stages of the processes are 
clearly articulated. 
c. Providers meet (where applicable) the national and international requirements of 
external bodies with responsibility for hearing or overseeing concerns and 
complaints. 
d. Actions resulting from concerns, complaints and appeals are proportionate and 
enable cases to be resolved as early as possible. 
e. Processes for concerns, complaints and appeals are monitored and reviewed to 
ensure they promote enhancement throughout the provider and operate as 
intended, to the benefit of students and staff. 
f. Outcomes from concerns, complaints and appeals are used to develop and 
enhance teaching and learning and the wider student experience. 
 
Student Conduct Regulations

COMSC School Handbook 25 26
Section 1 Introduction 
Welcome to your student handbook, which explains how the university works. It is split into 
two sections: 
1) The first covers: 
- how your degree works 
- the facilities and services available 
- how to give feedback or report a concern 
- the rules, regulations, and policies you must follow. 
2) the second part includes information on your school and/or programme. 
The information linked to in both parts is updated regularly. If, having read this handbook you 
have questions, contact Student Connect or your school.

COMSC School Handbook 25 26
Section 2 Welcome to Cardiff University 
We're delighted to welcome you to our community. You are now part of an ambitious and 
innovative university: 
- founded in 1883 
- bilingual in Welsh and English 
- home to over 32,000 students and 7,000 staff from nearly 140 countries 
- teaching more than 20 subject areas 
- with 24 academic schools across three colleges. 
 
 
''A warm welcome to your university - wherever you're based and whatever you're studying 
we have so much to offer. This handbook gives you the key information you need about 
studying here, the support available, and how to make the most of your university 
experience. 
Our student community is the heart of Cardiff University, and we welcome students from all 
over the world. There are many educational, social, cultural, and sporting experiences on 
offer to you through the university and Students' Union. To keep you updated on important 
news and exciting opportunities, I will write to you on a regular basis, and we hope that you 
enjoy your time with us.'' 
Claire Morgan, Pro-Vice Chancellor Education and Student Experience 
 
'As your Students' Union President, I am so excited to welcome both new and returning 
students to Cardiff this year! I hope this handbook will show you how to make the most of 
both your academic and student life during your time here.' 
Maria Pollard, Students' Union President

COMSC School Handbook 25 26
Section 2.1 The Student Charter 
It is important you read the Student Charter and understand how it applies to you. 
Created with students, the Students' Union and the university, it outlines mutual expectations 
and what to do if they aren't met.

2.2 Being at a Welsh university 
In Wales, Welsh and English are both official languages. We hope you will embrace the Welsh 
language and culture while at Cardiff. 
For students who are Welsh speakers there are opportunities available for you to use and 
enhance your Welsh language skills - academically, professionally and socially. 
If you are not a Welsh speaker, there are opportunities for you to learn Welsh for free alongside 
your studies. Croeso i Gaerdydd / Croeso (welcome) to Cardiff!

COMSC School Handbook 25 26
Section 2.3 Students' Union 
Cardiff Students' Union (CSU) is at the heart of Cardiff student life. That means that CSU is 
here to support students to thrive and to have their backs when things don't go as planned, all 
within a safe, inclusive space where students can be who they want to be. CSU is consistently 
ranked in the top three for student satisfaction in the UK and was voted top 2 in the WhatUni 
Student Choice Awards for the last four years (2022-2025). 
As soon as you enrol as a student, you automatically become a member of the student 
community 
at 
CSU. 
With 
close 
to 
200 societies, 
74 sports 
clubs and 
lots 
of volunteering opportunities, there is plenty to get involved in. CSU also works with you in all 
aspects of your academic life, gives advice and support when you need it, and offers 
unforgettable experiences and exceptional events to help expand your community in Cardiff.

COMSC School Handbook 25 26
Section 2.4 Equality, diversity, and inclusion 
Find out about the support available to students, along with policies, procedures and guidance 
on equality, diversity and inclusion.

2.5 Sustainability 
Get involved in sustainability activities to help reduce our carbon footprint and add green skills 
to your CV.

COMSC School Handbook 25 26
Section 2.6 Freedom of speech and planning events 
The principles of freedom of speech, freedom of expression and academic expression are 
important to us as an academic institution. However, we are bound by legislation to ensure 
these principles are exercised in compliance with laws protecting national security and public 
safety, preventing disorder or crime, and protecting the legal rights of others (for example, in 
relation to harassment and discrimination).

Section 3 Getting started 


3.1 Orientation 
Make sure you have completed orientation. If you have not received an email from 
welcome@cardiff.ac.uk for the orientation platform contact Student Connect.

3.2 Registration and enrolment 
You should have completed online enrolment. This includes confirming your personal and 
study details, who pays your fees and other essential information. 
If you are a home student you must complete these steps to trigger the release of your student 
loan (if you have applied for one). 
If you did not complete online enrolment before arriving in Cardiff and need assistance, visit 
our student ID card collection point.

COMSC School Handbook 25 26
Section 3.3 Student ID card 
Collection of your student ID card is a mandatory step in the enrolment process for campusbased students. As well as proof of identity, your ID card provides library and e-learning 
access and entry to university buildings. 
It will be valid for the duration of your studies, and you must carry it with you on campus. You 
can also access a digital version of your ID card via our Student App. 
If your ID card is lost, stolen or damaged you can request a replacement at the Centre for 
Student Life. 
If you are a distance-learning student, a student ID card is not required.

3.4 Your student record 
The Student Information Management System (SIMS) is our tool for managing student 
records. It is the portal you use to enrol, choose modules, and pay fees, and stores your: 
- personal details and contact information

- academic information 
- module and programme information. 
 
 
You must keep your record up to date so we have your: 
- mobile telephone number 
- home and term-time address 
- trusted contact information 
- preferred name 
- changes to your programme of study/modules. 
You can amend your student record or request confirmation of your student status via SIMS. 
We also encourage you to disclose your equality data. This helps us see where there may be 
differences of experience or barriers, and may be used by authorised groups to help improve 
the inclusivity and diversity of our services. Our equality monitoring data is reported 
anonymously in our annual monitoring report. 
Our data protection notice explains how we use your data, and how it is kept secure. 
Data protection legislation gives you certain rights in relation to the information we hold about 
you, such as requesting a copy of the personal data we hold for you. Not all information held 
will be considered your personal data and you may not be entitled to receive all the information 
you request, such as, only being entitled to receive exam scripts where there are additional 
comments made by the marker (see marking and moderation policy for details). Contact the 
Compliance and Risk team for more information.

COMSC School Handbook 25 26
Section 3.5 Payment of fees 
You are required to pay tuition fees, or provide evidence of sponsorship, for each year of your 
course (including repeat years). 
If paying your tuition fees via SIMS, ensure you are ready to make the payment before 
continuing to the fee payment stage of the task. Once you reach this step, you will be unable 
to save and exit, or continue without making the payment, and you will need to seek support 
from your school.

COMSC School Handbook 25 26

The academic regulations handbook explains the rules and regulations governing your 
programme. These are supplemented by several policies and processes that will support you 
through your studies. 
The regulations are reviewed frequently, and students are consulted on the impact of any 
proposed changes to regulations. As a student enrolled on a programme with us, you agree 
to abide by our academic regulations, so it is important that you familiarise yourself with them

and with the range of policies and procedures that underpin them. Section 9 has further

3.7 Library services 
Our Library staff and facilities provide resources, support and a welcoming environment to 
help you learn. You can study at any library on our campuses, no matter what course you are 
studying. 
 
You'll also have access to tools and support through our live chat service. Each academic 
school has subject librarians who also provide support and training. 
Use the LibrarySearch catalogue to find and access print and online resources and to check 
your library account. The Lean Library plugin gives you seamless access to resources when 
working away from our campuses. Visit Welcome to the Library for more information.

All students using our IT facilities are bound by the university IT regulations, which are

Eduroam is a fully secured, on-campus wireless network, available to students after

If you have trouble connecting, or need quick and easy access to the internet for a short time, 
you can use your university email address and password to connect to CU-Wireless (not 
available in some Cardiff and Vale Health Board locations). 
The CU-PSK network allows you to connect gaming consoles and smart speakers to the WiFi from university accommodation, however not all devices and games are compatible with 
the network.

Keep in touch using Microsoft Teams, and learn how to keep your video calls secure.

- Access in-person IT support in the Centre for Student Life 
- For urgent enquiries call us 24/7 on +44 (0)29 2251 1111 (some requests may not be 
resolvable on weekdays between 17:00 and 08:00, during weekends, and bank

Section 3.13 Protect yourself and your data online 
Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) helps keep your data and account secure. You will need to 
set up MFA before you can access many University systems, including your timetable, the 
intranet, and Microsoft 365 account. Protect yourself, your information and devices by: 
- installing anti-virus software and keeping it up to date. If you do not have your own, 
you can download free anti-virus software 
- setting a strong password. Do not reuse a password on multiple sites. You can reset 
your password online 
- ensuring your devices are lockable, protected, and having the latest operating system 
and security patches 
- being aware of fraudulent emails, phone calls, and text messages, and how to keep 
yourself safe from scams and fraud 
- using our virtual private network (VPN) if you need secure access to on-campus 
resources 
- telling IT Support if you have clicked on a link or entered any details in a suspiciouslooking email.

COMSC School Handbook 25 26
Section 3.14 Communications 
It is important to keep up to date with university news and events by checking your university 
email regularly and downloading our Student App. Our student communications commitment 
explains how we will communicate with you and you can view a list of the channels we'll use. 
Your student intranet has information, advice, services, and applications and it is here to help 
with all aspects of student life.

4 How your degree works 


4.1 Programme information 
SIMS has information about your programme including teaching, assessments and learning 
outcomes. 
Programme handbooks and descriptions of your modules are available on Learning Central.

COMSC School Handbook 25 26
Section 4.2 Module options 
Sometimes reasonable changes will be made to your programme, as per the terms and 
conditions of your offer. More information can be found in the Variation of Arrangements 
statement in our academic regulations.

4.2 Module options 
Module options may be limited due to timetable clashes, places available or a minimum 
number of sign-ups to run. Some modules are mandatory for all students on a programme or 
require prior learning. You can seek advice on module choices from your personal tutor.

COMSC School Handbook 25 26
Section 4.3 Blended Learning 
We take a blended learning approach to our teaching that combines in-person and online 
engagement and activities. To help you make the most of the digital tools and platforms 
available, we have created the Blended Learning at Cardiff University resource. 
Find more information about specific tools and platforms on the student intranet.

COMSC School Handbook 25 26
Section 4.4 Learning Central 
Learning Central is our virtual learning environment. It will be used to deliver your course 
content, activities and assessment. It provides information and tools to support your 
programme, including details about your teaching team, learning materials, and online 
assessments. 
Find out more about using Learning Central from our help guide.

COMSC School Handbook 25 26
Section 4.5 The purpose of assessment 
Assessments allow you to demonstrate your understanding, knowledge and skills, and 
evidence you have met the learning outcomes of your unit of study. They help staff and 
students monitor learning, whilst providing measures of achievement. 
1) Formative assessments: help you learn more effectively through feedback on your 
performance, indicating how you can improve. It does not count towards your overall 
mark. 
2) Summative assessment: used to indicate how well you have met the intended 
learning outcomes of a module or programme. It does count towards your overall mark. 
Feedback is provided for all work no later than 20 working days after the assessment 
deadline.

4.6 Assessments 
You may be required to submit coursework, presentations, blogs or videos for assessment - 
guidance can be found on Learning Central.

COMSC School Handbook 25 26
Section 4.7 Examinations 
All exam timetables are published on the student intranet and student timetabling system. 
Notification will be sent, approximately six weeks before the start of the exam period. Resit 
timetables are published two weeks before. Once published, your individual exam information 
can be found on your timetable.

COMSC School Handbook 25 26
Section 4.8 Marking 
Most assessment tasks require academic and/or professional judgement, which are supported 
by assessment criteria and/or mark schemes. 
Most summative assessments are marked anonymously. Results are overseen by examining 
boards, which may include external examiners to help monitor and judge standards. 
Word limits and assessment deadlines must be adhered to. 
In cases where coursework is submitted late, and where there are no extenuating 
circumstances: 
- if the assessment is submitted no later than 24 hours after the deadline, the mark for 
the assessment will be capped at the minimum pass mark 
- if the assessment is submitted more than 24 hours after the deadline, a mark of 0 will 
be given. 
 
Find out more about what to expect from feedback on your assessments. 
Your programme has an external examiner whose role it is to ensure that quality and 
standards are upheld. You can access external examiner reports from the last 5 years using 
your university login details.

COMSC School Handbook 25 26
Section 4.9 Assessment results 
Provisional assessment results will be made available on SIMS after an assessment has been 
marked. These are subject to confirmation by the relevant examining board. 
Once your results have been confirmed by an examining board, you will receive your interim 
transcript via email. Results are also available to view on SIMS. You can appeal against your 
results within 28 days of receiving your transcript via email. Your transcript also has 
information about academic appeals. 
If, having received your results, you need further information and support, you should contact 
your home school or personal tutor in the first instance. You can also contact the Student 
Connect team in the Centre for Student Life and Student Advice in the Students' Union.

COMSC School Handbook 25 26
Section 4.10 Feedback on assessment 
How we feedback is outlined in our academic feedback policy. Make the most of your feedback 
by learning how to recognise it and use it effectively.

5 Making changes to your module or programme 


5.1 Module transfers 
You can only request to change modules within 14 days of the start of teaching, in accordance 
with specific regulations that relate to your programme and year. Any changes to module must 
be approved by the school(s) who teach them. Your personal tutor or another staff member in 
your school will be able to advise you.

COMSC School Handbook 25 26
Section 5.2 Programme transfers 
You may be able to transfer to another programme, subject to meeting eligibility requirements 
and approval from the relevant school(s). This change must be made within 14 days of the 
start of teaching.

5.3 Student academic representation 
There are over 1,000 student representatives in the university. They bring your feedback to 
Student-Staff Panels, where staff, academic reps, and students discuss feedback and review 
proposals for changes. They can also signpost you to the range of support available to you. 
Find out who your rep is and how to become a rep.

COMSC School Handbook 25 26
Section 5.4 College Forums 
Issues that affect your College are discussed at College Forums, held once each semester.

6 Welsh language 
We are committed to creating the best possible Welsh language student experience whilst 
ensuring your rights under the Welsh Language Standards are met. We offer a range of 
subjects where students can study through the medium of Welsh, or partly in Welsh. We also 
offer the Cardiff Citizen module to all first-year students, if you tell us at enrolment that you 
have Welsh-language skills. Students can have access to a Welsh-speaking personal tutor 
and can submit assignments through the medium of Welsh, regardless of whether the course 
or module is taught in English. Scholarships, career advice, and disability and dyslexia advice 
are also available for students studying through the medium of Welsh.

COMSC School Handbook 25 26
Section 6.1 Learn Welsh Cardiff 
Learning Welsh allows students to develop a greater linguistic awareness and become a part 
of the Welsh culture within the university, the capital city, and Wales. Learn Welsh Cardiff 
provides free Welsh courses for all, from complete beginners to fluent Welsh speakers to 
increase their confidence.

COMSC School Handbook 25 26
Section 6.2 Coleg Cymraeg Cenedlaethol Welsh Language Skills Certificate 
The Welsh Language Skills Certificate qualification provides evidence of your level of Welshlanguage skills, and of your ability to use Welsh in the workplace. It is also supported by a 
Welsh Language Tutor and offers study skills support. Register through the Cardiff Coleg 
Cymraeg Branch by emailing cangen@caerdydd.ac.uk.
section_heading: Coleg Cymraeg Cenedlaethol Welsh Language Skills Certificate

text:
COMSC School Handbook 25 26
Section 6.3 Undeb Myfyrwyr Cymraeg Caerdydd 
Undeb Myfyrwyr Cymraeg Caerdydd (UMCC) in the Students' Union is responsible for 
representing Welsh speakers, learners, and anyone interested in the Welsh language and 
culture at Cardiff University. It is governed by students and works with Welsh students and 
societies to guarantee that events and services are offered to Welsh-speaking students. 
The Vice President Cymraeg is elected by students and represents the Welsh Language 
community as part of the full-time Sabbatical Officer team that leads the Students' Union.

COMSC School Handbook 25 26
Section 7 Your support services and looking after yourself 


7.1 Student Connect 
If you need support contact Student Connect. You can: 
- visit the Student Connect desk in the Centre for Student Life 
- use the Student Connect portal 
- use the chatbot when you are logged into the student intranet by clicking the blue and 
white chat button on the bottom right-hand corner of your screen 
- phone +44 (0)29 2251 8888.
section_heading: Your support services and looking after yourself

text:
COMSC School Handbook 25 26
Section 7.2 Feeling unwell, reporting an absence and having a trusted contact 
Make sure you are registered with a doctor. If you feel unwell contact your doctor, NHS Wales 
or other agencies responsible for providing care to you when needed. The university, as a 
provider of higher education, does not have the expertise or capacity to closely monitor 
students' mental or physical health, nor provide health care. 
 
If the university becomes aware that you are unwell, and has concerns for your welfare, we 
may engage a third party to help. To support this, we ask you to provide details of a trusted 
contact in SIMS. 
 
If you are unwell and unable to attend in-person teaching, you should inform your school from 
the first day of absence or as soon as possible thereafter. 
- If you are absent for more than 7 consecutive working days: speak to your 
personal tutor or staff in your school office. Absence due to illness for periods longer 
than seven consecutive days must be supported by a medical certificate, provided and 
signed by a medical practitioner, GP or doctor.
section_heading: Feeling unwell, reporting an absence and having a trusted contact

text:
- If you are absent for 14 days or more: you will need to apply for an interruption of 
study or extenuating circumstances, unless you have submitted a programme transfer, 
or you may be requested to withdraw. 
If you are unwell and have an upcoming assessment, you can use the extenuating 
circumstances process. 
If you have queries, speak to your personal tutor, school office or Student Connect. Impartial 
advice is also available from Student Advice in the Students' Union. 
Further information regarding absences is available in the academic regulations handbook. 
International students with a Student Visa who withdraw from their course or take an 
interruption of study of more than 60 days will be reported to the UK Home Office, which will 
result in their visa being cancelled. If you are an international student considering either 
withdrawing or taking an interruption of studies, contact Student Visa Support.

COMSC School Handbook 25 26
Section 7.3 Health, wellbeing and safety 
Our dedicated Health and Wellbeing team is here to help you look after yourself while at 
university. We offer a wide range of self-help resources, along with workshops, courses, 
therapeutic groups, events, peer support, and professional one-to-one appointments all 
designed to help you manage your emotional, mental, and physical health. 
If you are concerned about your personal safety, or have experienced an incident of violence 
and abuse, get urgent advice. 
Our health, safety, and environment policies are in place to support and protect students, staff 
and our environment. The Health and Safety at Work Act provides a legal framework for 
safety regulations. 
You should report any accident or incident which happens on university premises or involves 
any individual engaged with Cardiff University business, whether in the UK or abroad. This 
helps us to learn lessons from incidents, and is designed to comply with the reporting of 
injuries, disease and dangerous occurrences regulations. 
We are committed to providing a safe and supportive learning environment. Equally, you have 
a responsibility for your own wellbeing. If you are unwilling or unable to manage your own 
wellbeing, and it is felt that there is good reason to intervene, we will do so in line with 
our student support intervention policy and procedure.

7.4 Report and Support 
We are committed to creating a safe, respectful, and inclusive community for all. Report and 
Support is a confidential and easy-to-use online tool for you to report incidents of: 
- assault 
- bullying

- discrimination 
- harassment 
- hate crime 
- sexual misconduct 
- and serious mental health concerns. 
You can make a report anonymously or give details about yourself or others. Choose the route 
that feels most comfortable for you, or the individual you are reporting for. You do not need to 
log-in to use Report and Support and all information will be treated sensitively and 
confidentially. All reports are handled by our trauma-informed specialist practitioners who are 
here to support you. 
If you or someone else is experiencing violence or abuse and are in immediate danger, call 
the emergency services on 999.

COMSC School Handbook 25 26
Section 7.5 University residences 
All residences have a Residences Management Team to support students in university 
accommodation. Learn more about living in residences, including community living, health and 
safety, room transfers, and leaving residences. 
Your Residence Life Team are also here to help you settle in, provide advice and assist with 
issues around community living. Join their free events and activities throughout the year and 
keep up to date through their website.

COMSC School Handbook 25 26
Section 7.6 Financial support and money advice 
The Advice and Money team are here to support you with your finances. They can help with 
budgeting, offer advice on funding and if you're running low on money while you're studying, 
they can help you access emergency assistance from the university's Money Support Fund 
(MSF). 
Contact the team via Student Connect or visit them in the Centre for Student Life.

COMSC School Handbook 25 26
Section 7.7 Multi-faith chaplaincy 
The Multi-faith chaplaincy is a place of friendship, hospitality, reflection, support, and dialogue. 
The chaplaincy provides spiritual pastoral care for students and staff, with or without faith.

7.8 Supporting your student life - equality, diversity and inclusion 
Additional support is available to you via Student Connect, including financial support and a 
dedicated contact, if your personal circumstances are listed below: 
- asylum seekers and refugees 
- care experienced 
- disability and dyslexia 
- estranged students

COMSC School Handbook 25 26
Section 7.9 Student parents 
- military experienced 
- gender reassignment 
- LGBTQ+ students 
- religion and belief 
- student carers.

7.9 Student parents 
If you already have a child or are about to become a parent, our Advice and Money team can 
help make sure you are receiving the funding you are entitled to and discuss any expected 
changes to your studies. 
Being pregnant, adopting, or caring for a child should not be a barrier to succeeding in your 
studies. If you need help in finding childcare or locating a school, Student Connect can 
signpost you to other services and organisations. 
The university has a registered Little Scholars Nursery for dependents of students and staff. 
Advice and assistance on bringing your family to the UK with you is available for international 
students via Student Connect.

COMSC School Handbook 25 26
Section 7.10 Student Advice - Students' Union 
Student Advice is a free, confidential, independent, and impartial advice service provided by 
the Students' Union, based on the third floor of the Students' Union building. 
 
Contact the Student Advice team through their website, by emailing advice@cardiff.ac.uk or 
by calling +44(0)29 2078 1410.

COMSC School Handbook 25 26
Section 7.11 Nightline 
Cardiff Nightline is a confidential, student-led, term-time listening service. It serves as a 
listening ear if you need someone to listen and help explore how you are feeling. 
 
The phoneline +44(0)29 2087 0555 is available Wednesdays and Saturdays from 20:0008:00. The Instant Messaging service is available from 08:00-00:00 on Wednesdays and 
Saturdays.

COMSC School Handbook 25 26
Section 7.12 Academic study skills 
We offer support to all undergraduate and postgraduate taught students to develop your skills 
in essay writing, note taking, and critical reading and thinking. Students can access this 
support via: 
- Classes lasting 50 minutes and involving discussion, interactive activities and question 
and answer sessions. Book a class.

- Resources to work through at your own pace, including handouts, templates to 
structure your work, recorded lectures, interactive tutorials, and videos to guide you 
through a range of topics. 
 
For more information, contact the Academic Study Skills and Mentoring team via Student 
Connect.

COMSC School Handbook 25 26
Section 7.13 Online resources 
Resources available to support the development of your study skills cover: 
- critical analysis 
- managing and citing information sources 
- academic writing 
- research skills, such as literature review and research methodology. 
Our Academic Study Skills module includes interactive tutorials to work through at your own 
pace and templates to help structure your work

COMSC School Handbook 25 26
Section 7.14 Disabled students 
Contact the Student Disability Service as early as possible to discuss your needs and the 
specialist support and adjustments that may be available to you.

7.15 Maths and statistics support 
The Maths Support Service is available to all students, with drop-in sessions, specialised 
workshops and online learning materials available.

COMSC School Handbook 25 26
Section 7.16 Learn a new language 
If you're interested in learning a new language or building on your existing skills, Uniwide 
Languages offers a variety of courses you can take alongside your studies.

7.17 English language support 
If English is not your first language, you can access tailored support to help develop your 
academic English skills, both in person and online.

COMSC School Handbook 25 26
Section 7.18 Study spaces 
Study spaces are available in all libraries, a selection of university buildings and the Student's 
Union without booking in advance. Choose from quiet areas, collaborative spaces, desks with 
or without electrical sockets, height-adjustable desks and open-access PCs.

COMSC School Handbook 25 26
Section 8 Your future career 
Student Futures provide employability support for students and recent graduates. This 
includes careers advice, CV and application support, skills development, careers fairs and 
events along with online tools and the Jobs Board. Manage bookings and browse jobs and 
opportunities on your Student Futures Account. 
If you are looking to work, study or volunteer abroad, or have an idea for starting your own 
business, our Global Opportunities and Enterprise and Start-up teams are here to help.

COMSC School Handbook 25 26
Section 8.1 Student Mentor Scheme 
The Student Mentor Scheme helps new students settle into university life. If you're a first-year 
undergraduate, you will be allocated a student mentor from your academic school. Once 
you've found your feet we'll be in touch with the opportunity to become a mentor, helping you 
to improve your employability skills and help incoming first-year undergraduate students.

COMSC School Handbook 25 26
Section 8.2 Your Higher Education Achievement Report 
When you graduate, many of your activities will be included in your Higher Education 
Achievement Report (HEAR). It's a digital record, allowing you to present your achievements 
to employers and further education providers.

8.3 Volunteering 
The Students' Union offers a wide variety of different and exciting volunteering opportunities. 
Volunteering is a great way to make a difference in your new community. You'll also gain skills 
that employers will look for, meet new people, and of course have lots of fun! 
You can also explore volunteering abroad with Global Opportunities. 
International students who need a visa to study in the UK should speak to Student Visa 
Support before volunteering as some activities may affect your working conditions.

COMSC School Handbook 25 26
Section 9 Academic Regulations 
As well as the information here, you will also need to refer to the academic regulations section 
in your academic school section of this handbook (section 17).

9.1 Attending lectures and completing work 
You are expected to: 
- attend all your programme activities 
- complete your assigned work 
- achieve satisfactory results in your assessed work 
- become an independent and self-directed learner.

If you fail to meet the attendance requirements of your course, you will receive a warning from 
the Head of School (or nominee). If you receive a warning and need advice, contact Student 
Connect or Student Advice. 
 
Further information is available in our student study and engagement regulations within 
the academic regulations handbook. 
 
Be aware that if you receive tuition fees from the Student Loans Company or a university 
bursary, you will be required to confirm your attendance during the year to ensure funds are 
released to you. International students with Student Visas who fail to meet attendance 
requirements will be reported to the UK Home Office. 
 
Check what to do if you feel unwell and how to report an absence. Information on extenuating 
circumstances can be found in section 9.4 or on the student intranet. If your mental health and 
wellbeing has impacted your workload and attendance, contact Student Connect for support.

COMSC School Handbook 25 26
Section 9.2 Seeking guidance and support 
If things aren't meeting your expectations, you should get in touch and raise your concerns 
with your personal tutor, Student Connect or Student Advice as soon as possible (within 28 
days) and seek advice if these are not resolved. You should inform us promptly if: 
- there are any changes to your circumstances 
- your own experience is adversely affected by the behaviour of fellow students or staff 
- your academic progress, or any other aspect of your experience, gives you cause for 
concern.

COMSC School Handbook 25 26
Section 9.3 Alternative examination arrangements 
You can apply for alternative arrangements that allow you to: 
- have reasonable adjustments. Apply as soon as you start university, if you can. The 
deadline for us to process arrangements is 8 weeks before your examination. 
- avoid religious observance days. If you are unable to sit an exam on a certain day or 
at a certain time you must let us know by week 3 of each semester. 
- sit your exams in Welsh 
- sit your examinations away from the university.

COMSC School Handbook 25 26
Section 9.4 Extenuating circumstances 
You are expected to submit all assessments by the published deadlines and attend 
assessment activities as scheduled. 
 
If you experience a severe and exceptional circumstance in the period immediately before, or 
during, an assessment, you must submit a declaration of extenuating circumstances to your 
school. 
 
To be considered as an extenuating circumstance, your situation must meet all of 
these criteria: 
- be severe and exceptional; and

- unforeseen or unavoidable; and 
- close in time to the assessment, or where you can demonstrate that the circumstances 
continued to have an impact on your ability to complete assessments or to undertake 
examinations. 
 
When you experience extenuating circumstances, you will usually be unable to complete the 
assessment as scheduled and must declare your circumstances before the assessment 
deadline. There are limited situations when you can declare extenuating circumstances after 
starting or having completed an assessment.

COMSC School Handbook 25 26
Section 9.5 Academic integrity 
It is essential that you understand what academic integrity is, and how to avoid academic 
misconduct. You must complete your assessments and exams honestly, fairly and 
respectfully. 
You can find guidance on artificial intelligence, academic integrity, contract cheating, 
plagiarism, collusion, and academic misconduct on the student intranet and links to complete 
an academic integrity module on Learning Central. 
Your subject librarian can also help with referencing queries. 
We use a range of different tools and techniques to identify academic misconduct. The 
penalties for students can be severe. Invigilators are also trained to identify misconduct in 
examinations. It is up to you to ensure that you don't commit an unfair practice, even 
unintentionally - it is an offence either way. Further information is available in our academic 
integrity policy.

COMSC School Handbook 25 26
Section 9.6 Student behaviour, conduct and discipline 
You are expected to demonstrate respect for the university, staff, fellow students, and the local 
community on and off campus. We operate a zero tolerance approach to behaviours of 
harassment, bullying and victimisation and are committed to establishing an inclusive culture, 
free from discrimination, and based on dignity, courtesy, and respect. 
If students behave in a way that contradicts this, we may act using the student conduct 
procedure and the Fitness to Practise procedure for students who are studying on 
programmes leading to professional registration. 
If you experience harassment, bullying, hate crime, violence or abuse use Report and Support 
to tell us what happened and access specialist support.

9.7 Student complaints procedure 
All students have the right to submit a complaint - either as an individual or as a group. 
Complaints must be raised within 28 days of the concern arising - or the latest occurrence of 
the incident if it's ongoing.

COMSC School Handbook 25 26
Section 9.8 Thinking of leaving 
Read our student complaint procedure to understand what you can submit a complaint about, 
the procedure for handling the complaint, possible outcomes and the complaint form.

9.8 Thinking of leaving 
If you are struggling with your course or finding it is not what you expected and you 
are considering withdrawing from your programme, discuss this first with your personal tutor, 
supervisor, school office, or the Advice and Money team or Student Advice. There are many 
people here to support you and explain your options (e.g. taking an interruption of study). 
If you are an international student and believe that withdrawing or taking an interruption of 
study may be the best option for you, discuss your situation with the Student Visa Support 
team first. If you withdraw or take an interruption of study, UK Visas and Immigration will expect 
you to return to your home country, as you were issued with a visa to study in the UK. You will 
need to make a new visa application when/if you choose to return to the UK to resume your 
studies.

COMSC School Handbook 25 26
Section 10 After you complete your degree 


10.1 Graduation 
Graduation is a time to celebrate your success alongside family and friends. Graduation 
events are held in July.

10.2 Graduate advice and support 
For three years after you graduate you can keep accessing career advice and support. This 
includes face-to-face consultations, mock interviews, CV checks, careers resources, jobspecific information, and a jobs board.

COMSC School Handbook 25 26
Section 10.3 Moving on to postgraduate study 
Considering continuing into further study after your undergraduate degree? We have a 
postgraduate community known globally for outstanding research and teaching, and you can 
receive an alumni discount.

10.4 Graduate Outcomes survey 
It's important that you enter a personal email address in SIMS as 15 months after your course 
ends you will be asked to complete a national survey called Graduate Outcomes. 
This UK government survey is sent to all UK University graduates. Your responses will help 
future students by evaluating your degree programme and contributing to the university's 
position in league tables.

COMSC School Handbook 25 26
Section 10.5 Requesting a reference 
If you require a reference for an application for a job or further study, ask your personal tutor.

10.6 Verification of study and replacement certificates 
Once your award has been conferred by the Awards and Progress Committee, you will receive 
a hard copy of your degree certificate. You can also access digital copies of your certificate 
and Higher Education Achievement Report via Verify and share these documents with third 
parties including employers and other Higher Education institutions. If your original degree 
certificate is lost or destroyed, you can request a replacement.

COMSC School Handbook 25 26
Section 11 Our alumni community 
Cardiff is for life! Even after you graduate, we're here for you. You'll join a global alumni 
community of over 200,000 and can access alumni support, benefits and discounts. Make 
sure you opt in to alumni communications when you enrol, and we'll keep you connected with 
your Cardiff community and up to date with news, opportunities and events.

COMSC School Handbook 25 26
Section 12 Welcome to the School of Computer Science and Informatics 
You are part of a vibrant community of undergraduate and postgraduate students pursuing 
taught degree programmes within the school. As you progress through your degree, you will 
find that your study is influenced by both the strong research of the school and the professional 
accreditation requirements of the British Computer Society and The Chartered Institute for IT. 
You can find out more about research in the school here. 
The school is one of seven academic schools within Cardiff University which make up the 
College of Physical Sciences & Engineering: a centre of academic excellence, internationally 
renowned for research and teaching excellence, innovation, industrial engagement, 
sustainable solutions, and societal impact. 
We're always keen to hear your thoughts about your experience studying with us. In this 
section of the handbook, you'll find information about who to contact within COMSC if you 
need advice, have a concern, or simply want to share something-whether it's a challenge or 
a success. 
 
 
Kathryn Jones 
Head of School 
JonesK90@cardiff.ac.uk

The Outreach Team regularly visit primary and secondary schools in the local area to inspire

The Technical Services Team manages the School's Workshop services, and also a Maker

and electronics prototyping equipment. 
We support students through the provision of non-IT technical equipment for
